hook_text: You can double the height of your water tank or double its width. One gives twice the water. The other gives four times.
clip_script: A tank holds about 2 124 litres. Option one: make it twice as tall. Volume is the floor times the height, so twice the height means twice the water, about 4 247 litres. Option two: make it twice as wide, doubling the radius. Now the floor is a circle that grows in both directions at once, twice as wide side to side and twice as wide front to back. That is four times the floor, so four times the water: about 8 495 litres. The radius counts twice because it is squared in pi r squared h. Double everything, radius and height, and you get eight times as much. And here is the bonus: the wide tank needs less plastic for every litre it holds. Lengths times 2, area times 4, volume times 8. Wider beats taller.
visual_style: A cylinder tank on a whiteboard; one copy stretches upward and fills to a doubled water line; another copy widens and fills to four times the level, with litre counters racing; a final tank doubles both ways and an eight appears.
pacing: Clear setup, a steady first option, a jump on the second, a quick finish on eight.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson for doubling prisms, surface area against volume and the scale factor k cubed.
